Agentic AI may extend these applications by autonomously planning, coordinating, and executing clinical and administrative workflows. However, empirical evidence on how healthcare professionals conceptualise agentic AI and anticipate its implications for work and occupational well-being remains limited. This study explores healthcare professionals' perceptions and expectations regarding agentic AI and its potential effects on healthcare work. Methods: We conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with 25 healthcare professionals from different clinical backgrounds in Germany. Interviews explored perceptions of agentic AI, focusing on workflow organisation, workload, professional autonomy, accountability, and occupational well-being. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke. Results: Five themes were identified: (1) from assisting decisions to organising work; (2) automation redistributes rather than removes work; (3) delegating action without delegating responsibility; (4) implications for working conditions and health- and work-related outcomes; and (5) meaningful human control requires organisational conditions. Participants distinguished between conventional AI-based decision support and more autonomous forms of AI in their accounts, using this contrast to describe potential changes in workflow organisation. Their accounts highlighted practical consequences of delegating workflow-related activities to AI systems, including changes in task structures, monitoring and verification demands, exception management, and the distribution of professional responsibility. Agentic AI may extend these applications by autonomously planning, coordinating, and executing clinical and administrative workflows. However, empirical evidence on how healthcare professionals conceptualise agentic AI and anticipate its implications for work and occupational well-being remains limited. This study explores healthcare professionals' perceptions and expectations regarding agentic AI and its potential effects on healthcare work. Methods: We conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with 25 healthcare professionals from different clinical backgrounds in Germany. Interviews explored perceptions of agentic AI, focusing on workflow organisation, workload, professional autonomy, accountability, and occupational well-being. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke. Results: Five themes were identified: (1) from assisting decisions to organising work; (2) automation redistributes rather than removes work; (3) delegating action without delegating responsibility; (4) implications for working conditions and health- and work-related outcomes; and (5) meaningful human control requires organisational conditions. Participants distinguished between conventional AI-based decision support and more autonomous forms of AI in their accounts, using this contrast to describe potential changes in workflow organisation. Their accounts highlighted practical consequences of delegating workflow-related activities to AI systems, including changes in task structures, monitoring and verification demands, exception management, and the distribution of professional responsibility. Participants anticipated reduced routine administrative workload and improved care coordination, but also potential increases in cognitive and supervisory demands. Conclusions: Agentic AI may shift healthcare from AI-assisted decision-making towards AI-mediated workflow execution. Its effects on occupational well-being may therefore be bidirectional, combining workload relief with increased cognitive and supervisory demands. Appropriate governance, clearly defined accountability, meaningful human oversight, workforce training, and regulatory alignment will be essential for responsible implementation.\", \"doi\": healthcare: a perspective on cognitive agency, skill evolution, and accountability.\", \"abstract\": \"Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) are transforming clinical decision support systems (CDSS) from traditional discrete predictions into fluent, context-aware clinical narrative generation. Although these capabilities substantially improve the efficiency of clinical workflows, they also introduce distinctive cognitive challenges: highly fluent and seemingly plausible medical narratives may reshape the way physicians construct clinical meaning and make analytic judgments. This perspective paper introduces the concept of Narrative Cognitive Substitution (NCS), proposed as a testable mid-level theoretical construct, which describes the hypothesized shift in human cognition from active hypothesis generation to passive retrospective validation when GenAI outputs pre-organize diagnostic reasoning and therapeutic pathways. We further propose a Skill Evolution Framework that characterizes the potential effects of GenAI on physician competence across five trajectories: Augmentation, Restructuring, Deskilling, Never-skilling, and Mis-skilling. In addition, we analyze the resulting Accountability Gap: although algorithmic outputs are increasingly embedded in clinical decision-making, decision influence is distributed across clinicians, institutions, developers, and deployers, yet professional accountability and final decision authority remain formally concentrated on the individual physician. To address these systemic challenges, we propose a human-centered governance framework -presented as design hypotheses requiring prospective evaluation- encompassing user interface design (embedding risk-adaptive cognitive friction), medical education (establishing targeted, protected AI-free reasoning exercises (\\\"Reasoning Cleanrooms\\\")), and institutional policies (implementing substantive human oversight and algorithmovigilance). We argue that the goal of digital health governance should not be to maximize automation, but rather to safeguard human cognitive agency, diagnostic vigilance, and layered, distributed accountability within AI-enabled healthcare systems.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fpubh.2026.1979099\", \"pmid\": \"42947839\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13710273\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1979099\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13710273\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13710273?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Cared for But Not Cared About? AI and the Moral Practice of Nursing.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence is increasingly deployed in healthcare not only to provide information or perform clinical tasks, but also to offer reassurance, companionship, and emotional support. This paper introduces the concept of engineered care to describe technological practices designed to generate the experiential effects of caregiving through system design rather than through the relational and moral practices that have traditionally constituted care. Its characteristic product is engineered comfort: the felt experience of reassurance, support, or being attended to that such systems can produce without assuming responsibility for the person receiving it. This comfort can be meaningful and may reduce distress, particularly where human care is scarce. The ethical challenge, therefore, is not simply that these systems fail, but that they succeed in producing experiences that resemble care. Drawing on care ethics, particularly Tronto's account of care as a moral practice, and on nursing's relational commitments, the paper argues that AI systems' growing capacity to produce comforting experiences risks redefining care as the delivery of desirable emotional outcomes. As reassurance and support become proxies for care, experiential indicators of success displace relational practices. Relational labor is increasingly delegated to technological systems, while responsibility for addressing the emotional and relational needs those systems leave unresolved continues to fall on nurses. Distinguishing engineered comfort from care enables nursing ethics to acknowledge these technologies' benefits without treating their experiential effects as equivalent to moral and relational practice.\", \"doi\": \"10.1111/nup.70135\", \"pmid\": \"42929698\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13701077\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1111/nup.70135\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13701077\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13701077?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "b3b64b81debaee2ed0dda9c864da56e790c4eedd46c99ec1982de0e118382184", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "responsibility_formation", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.3390/healthcare14203386", "doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1979099", "doi:10.1111/nup.70135", "pmc:PMC13704506", "pmc:PMC13658564", "pmc:PMC13710273", "pmc:PMC13701077"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.3390/healthcare14203386", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13704506", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13704506?pdf=render", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13658564/?tool=EBI", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13658564/pdf/?tool=EBI", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13658564", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13658564?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1979099"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
